justice: Most of the visible street space is allocated to motor traffic, while there is no clearly built sidewalk on either side of the road.
The left side is occupied by a green construction/industrial fence and parked forklifts, limiting shared access to public edge space.
The right side is partly taken by a large parked truck and an unpaved shoulder, reducing equal usability for non-motorized users.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked pedestrian crossings, or other barrier-free features are visible in the scene.
safety: A large truck is parked on the right shoulder and forklifts are parked on the left roadside, creating roadside hazards and potential sight obstructions.
There is no visible separated pedestrian path or protected bicycle lane, so vulnerable road users would need to mix with motor traffic.
The road is relatively wide and straight, which can encourage higher vehicle speeds in the absence of visible traffic calming devices.
Lane edge markings are present and daytime visibility is good, offering some basic guidance for drivers.
livability: The street appears industrial and vehicle-oriented, with warehouses/factory buildings and very limited signs of active public life.
No benches, bus stops, storefronts, public gathering spaces, or recreational elements are visible along the corridor.
The roadside edges are dominated by fencing, trucks, utility poles, and service space rather than community-serving amenities.
Tree cover exists mainly on the right side, but it does not translate into an active or sociable street environment.
sustainability: Rows of mature trees on the right and farther ahead provide some ecological value and limited shade.
However, the street design prioritizes motor vehicles, with no visible transit stop, dedicated cycling facility, or pedestrian-supportive green infrastructure.
Large paved carriageway surfaces and industrial roadside uses suggest a high car/truck dependence pattern.
No visible bioswales, permeable paving, rain gardens, or stormwater management features can be identified.
aesthetics: The continuous line of green trees on the right side softens the corridor and improves visual quality.
The roadway is relatively clean and uncluttered in the travel lane, which supports a basic sense of order.
At the same time, parked trucks, forklifts, overhead utility wires, and long metal fencing create a utilitarian industrial appearance.
The scene lacks pedestrian-scale design features, facade detail, and public-space elements that would make the streetscape more visually engaging.
comfort: Thermal comfort is uneven: trees on the right provide some shade, but much of the road and roadside remains exposed to sun and heat.
Physical comfort for non-drivers is poor because there is no visible sidewalk, seating, or protected waiting area.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the presence of heavy vehicles such as the large truck and forklifts along the roadside.
The smooth asphalt surface benefits vehicle ride quality, but it does little to improve comfort for people walking or cycling.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, forcing pedestrians to use narrow shoulders or the road edge.
There are no marked crosswalks, curb extensions, refuge islands, or pedestrian signals visible in this segment.
Roadside obstacles such as parked trucks, forklifts, rough shoulder areas, and fencing make walking routes feel incomplete and exposed.
The long straight roadway with sparse street activity provides little pedestrian interest or enclosure.
bikeability: There is no dedicated or protected bike lane visible on either side of the street.
Cyclists would need to share space with trucks, cars, and industrial roadside activity, which increases stress and conflict risk.
The parked truck on the right and forklifts on the left narrow the effective roadside operating space for cycling.
While the pavement appears relatively smooth, the absence of markings, protection, and bicycle parking keeps cycling suitability very low.
